messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Entrapment: Having no options, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Phong was seventy when he volunteered as a data analyst for a humanitarian organization in a contested region of the Middle East. What began as a desk job ended abruptly when his convoy was ambushed on a supply run. He spent six hours pinned in a collapsed clinic with two wounded colleagues, listening to gunfire and the shouts of armed men who ransacked the supplies. One of the men, a young fighter, laughed as he kicked a dying medic. Phong could not move, could not help, could only press himself against the cold floor and wait. That moment—the laughter, the helplessness, the stench of blood and diesel—never left him.

In the months after returning home, the memory did not fade. It intruded without warning: the feel of the concrete against his cheek, the crack of a rifle, the medic’s shallow breaths. When the memory surfaced, it felt as though he were still in that clinic—not remembering, but reliving. The scene would play over and over, a film he could not stop. At first he tried to push it away, but the images kept coming, especially at night. He began waking from nightmares with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, the dream residue clinging to him like smoke. Those mornings were the worst: he would lie still, certain that if he opened his eyes he would see the ceiling of the clinic, not his bedroom.

The waking moments after a nightmare were powerful triggers. They brought the memory roaring back, and they also fed his darkest fear: that his mind was unraveling. He began to believe that his reactions meant he was going crazy. He also grew terrified of his own anger. Once, while waiting in line at the grocery store, a customer cursed at the cashier—a small thing, but Phong felt a surge of rage so sudden and intense that he feared he might lash out physically. He retreated, shaking, convinced that he could lose control and do something terrible. The world, he concluded, was a dangerous place, and he was a danger too.

To manage these fears, Phong adopted a series of careful strategies. He avoided news reports of any conflict, turning off the television the moment a war zone appeared. He rehearsed conversations before every interaction, running through possible questions and his responses, because he was terrified that an unexpected comment might trigger his rage or reveal his instability. In public, he constantly scanned his environment, checking doorways, scanning faces for signs of threat. This hypervigilance kept his body on constant alert—shoulders tight, jaw clenched, ready to react to nothing.

Yet the very acts of rehearsing and scanning kept the memory alive. When he rehearsed a conversation, his mind would drift back to the clinic, as if the mental vigilance itself summoned the images. The checking behavior also increased his sense of being trapped: every scan of a room reminded him that he was always on guard, always without options. He came to see his own strategies as part of the threat—they confirmed that the world was unsafe and that he was barely holding on.

He noticed that his irritability had grown. A neighbor’s loud music, a delay in a software update—small frustrations triggered angry outbursts that frightened him. He would then avoid human contact, canceling plans with his adult children, telling himself he needed to protect them from his temper. His job as a data scientist, once a source of pride, became grueling: data sets required intense focus, but he could not concentrate. He spent hours rerunning the same analysis, because every time he tried to work, the memory of the clinic would surface, and he would lose his train of thought.

The cycle tightened. A news headline (trigger) would spark the memory, which reinforced his appraisal that the world was dangerous, which led him to scan his surroundings (maladaptive strategy), which in turn made him feel trapped, which made him think of the clinic again. Each component fed the next, and he became a prisoner of his own vigilance.

Now, at eighty, Phong has been retired for two years, but the symptoms have not lessened. He reaches for the remote every time a news broadcast begins. He rehearses the simplest phone calls. His children have stopped visiting as frequently, unsure how to reach him. What finally brought him to therapy was a morning when he woke from a nightmare and could not, for several seconds, remember where he was. He had come to believe that he was losing his mind, and he was terrified of the anger he felt toward a stranger who had cut him off in traffic. He hopes that naming the fear might loosen its grip, but he is not certain that talking about the clinic will help—or that he can bear to revisit it.
